subject: physics
title: Superposition and interference
key_idea: When waves meet, their displacements add. Waves from coherent sources interfere to give a stable pattern: constructive at path difference nλ and destructive at (n + ½)λ. Young's double slit gives light fringes with λ = ax / D.

blocks.text: When two or more waves meet at a point, they pass through each other and carry on unchanged. Where they meet, their effects add.

items.meaning: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of the separate waves at that point.
A line or surface joining points of a wave that are at the same stage of their oscillation.

items.text: Draw the two waves on the same axes, with the same x-axis.
Pick positions along the axis, such as every crest, trough and zero crossing.
At each position, add the two displacements with their signs.
Plot each sum and join the points with a smooth curve.

items: Crest meeting crest gives a bigger crest. Trough meeting crest of equal size gives zero.
Displacements in opposite directions subtract.
Resultant displacement = sum of the separate displacements, with signs.
Waves pass through one another and are not changed afterwards.

blocks.text: Interference is the effect of superposition when the waves come from sources that keep the same phase relationship.

items.meaning: The formation of regions of increased and decreased amplitude where waves from coherent sources overlap.
Sources that emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.
The difference in the distances from two sources to a point.
How far one wave is ahead of the other at a point, as an angle or fraction of a cycle.

blocks.label: Phase and path difference
where: phase difference = the angle between the waves (rad)
path difference = difference in distance travelled (m)

items: Two independent light sources are not coherent, because their phase relationship changes randomly many times a second.
Coherent light can come from one source split in two, or from a laser.
Constructive: path difference nλ. Destructive: path difference (n + ½)λ.
Interference needs coherent sources.

sections.heading: Two-source experiments and Young's double slit

blocks.text: Two-source interference can be shown with any type of wave. You look for a pattern of maxima and minima that stays still.

items: Water waves: two dippers in a ripple tank give lines of large and small ripples.
Sound: two loudspeakers on the same signal generator. Walking across in front of them, the sound rises and falls in loudness.
Microwaves: two slits in a metal plate in front of one transmitter. A probe moved along a line finds alternating maxima and minima.
Light: a laser shone through two slits, or a single source passing through a single slit and then two slits, gives bright and dark fringes.

blocks.text: For light, the two slits act as coherent sources, because both are lit by the same wavefront.

items: Light from the slits overlaps and meets on a screen at a distance D.
Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves add and there is a bright fringe.
Where it is an odd number of half wavelengths, they cancel and there is a dark fringe.
The fringes are equally spaced when a ≪ D.

blocks.label: Double-slit equation
where: D = distance from slits to screen (m)

diagram.alt: Calculate the fringe spacing on a screen from the wavelength, slit separation and distance.
diagram.question: Light of wavelength {lam} nm passes through two slits {a} mm apart. The screen is {D} m from the slits. Calculate the fringe spacing in mm.

items: White light gives a white central fringe with coloured fringes on each side. Each colour has its own fringe spacing, with blue closer in than red.
Young's experiment showed light interfering, which gave a classical confirmation of its wave nature.
Fringes need coherent sources: one wavefront through two slits.
λ = ax / D, with fringe spacing x measured between neighbouring bright fringes.

checks.q: State the condition for destructive interference between two coherent waves in terms of path difference.
checks.a: The path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths: (n + ½)λ.

checks.q: Explain why two filament lamps cannot be used as the sources in a double-slit experiment.
checks.a: They are not coherent: the phase difference between their waves changes randomly, so no stable interference pattern forms.

checks.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm is used with slits 0.50 mm apart and a screen 2.0 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing.

items: The fringe spacing is written w = λD / s, where s is the slit separation. It is the same relationship as λ = ax / D.
Laser safety: never look into a laser beam or its direct reflections. Use a low-power laser and keep the beam below eye level.
White light gives a central white fringe with coloured fringes either side, because each colour has a different wavelength.
Understanding of the nature of electromagnetic radiation has changed over time: Newton's particle model, Young's wave evidence, and later the photon model.
Describe and explain interference with sound and with electromagnetic waves, using path difference.

blocks.text: To see two-source fringes, these conditions must be met.

items: The sources must be coherent.
The waves must overlap, and must have similar amplitudes for clear fringes.
The waves must be unpolarised or polarised in the same plane.
The slit separation must be very small compared with D.
λ = ax / D applies to all waves, provided a ≪ D.
Use the principle of superposition to explain experiments with sound, light and microwaves.
Use research on the ideas of Newton and Huygens about the nature of light: Newton favoured a stream of particles, Huygens a wave.
